specStatements.text: The complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas in physics.

These key ideas are of universal application, and we have embedded them throughout the subject content. They underpin many aspects of the science assessment and will therefore be assessed across all papers.
• the use of models, as in the particle model of matter or the wave models of light and of sound
• the concept of cause and effect in explaining such links as those between force and acceleration, or between changes in atomic nuclei and radioactive emissions
• the phenomena of ‘action at a distance’ and the related concept of the field as the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects
• that differences, for example between pressures or temperatures or electrical potentials, are the drivers of change
• that proportionality, for example between weight and mass of an object or between force and extension in a spring, is an important aspect of many models in science
• that physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form.

concepts.definition: One of a small number of ideas used to describe the complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world. A key idea is a way of thinking that recurs across the whole subject rather than a detail belonging to one topic.

The property of the key ideas that they apply everywhere in the subject content rather than in one topic. Because they are embedded throughout the content, they underpin the assessment and are assessed across all papers.

A simplified representation of a system or process, used to describe, explain and predict behaviour. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by whether it contains every detail of the real thing.
A model in which matter is treated as a large number of small particles, with the arrangement and motion of those particles used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

A model in which a phenomenon is treated as a wave, so that quantities such as wavelength, frequency and amplitude can be used. Light is modelled as a transverse wave and sound as a longitudinal wave.
The idea that a change in one quantity produces a particular change in another: a resultant force causes acceleration, and a change inside an atomic nucleus causes a radioactive emission.
A phenomenon in which one object affects another without touching it, such as two magnets repelling, a charged rod attracting paper, or the Earth pulling on the Moon.

A region in which an object experiences a force because of a property it has, such as charge, magnetism or mass. The field concept is the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects.

A difference in a quantity between two places that causes something to change or to flow. A pressure difference drives gas flow, a temperature difference drives energy transfer by heating, and a potential difference drives charge flow.
A relationship in which one quantity changes by the same factor as another, so that the ratio of the two stays constant. Proportionality is an important aspect of many models in science.

The relationship shown by a graph that is a straight line through the origin. Weight is directly proportional to mass, and the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.

The expression of a physical law or model as an equation relating quantities, for example weight = mass × gravitational field strength. The equation states the relationship itself, not merely a recipe for a calculation.

misconceptions.question: What is a model in physics?
misconceptions.correct: A simplified representation used to describe, explain and predict behaviour; it may be an idea or an equation rather than an object.
misconceptions.misconception: A model is a small physical copy of the real thing, like a model aeroplane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language a model is a scaled-down object, and the first models many students meet in school are physical demonstrations.
misconceptions.correction: The particle model of matter and the wave models of light and of sound are ideas, not objects. They earn their place because they explain observations and predict new ones.

misconceptions.question: Does a useful model have to include every detail of the real thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. A model is deliberately simplified, and it is judged by how well it explains and predicts.
misconceptions.misconception: A model that leaves something out has been shown to be wrong and should be abandoned.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat science as a collection of true statements, so any simplification looks like an error rather than a deliberate choice.
misconceptions.correction: Every model has limits. The particle model treats particles as tiny spheres with no internal structure; that simplification is what makes the model useful, and its limits show where a better model is needed.

misconceptions.question: How does the wave model describe sound compared with light?
misconceptions.correct: Sound is modelled as a longitudinal wave; light is modelled as a transverse wave.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound and light are both modelled as transverse waves, because both are drawn as wavy lines.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show sound as a wavy oscilloscope trace, which looks transverse even though the oscillation is along the direction of travel.
misconceptions.correction: The oscilloscope trace is a graph of pressure against time, not a picture of the wave. In sound the particles oscillate along the direction of energy transfer, so the wave is longitudinal.

misconceptions.question: What is the effect of a constant resultant force on an object that is already moving?
misconceptions.correct: The object accelerates for as long as the resultant force acts.
misconceptions.misconception: A constant force makes an object move at a constant speed, and the object stops the moment the force is removed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience involves friction, so a steady push really does give a steady speed and things really do stop when you stop pushing.
misconceptions.correction: In those everyday cases the resultant force is zero, because friction balances the push. A non-zero resultant force is the cause and acceleration is the effect.

misconceptions.question: What causes an unstable nucleus to emit radiation?
misconceptions.correct: A change in the nucleus itself.
misconceptions.misconception: Radioactive emission is caused by conditions outside the atom, such as heating the sample or reacting it chemically.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every other change students meet, such as melting, dissolving and burning, is controlled by external conditions, so they transfer that expectation to decay.
misconceptions.correction: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process. Heating, cooling or chemically reacting a sample does not change its rate of decay, because the cause lies inside the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Do two magnets need a material between them in order to repel each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. A magnetic field acts through air and through a vacuum.
misconceptions.misconception: The air between the magnets is squashed and it is the air that pushes them apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a contact-force explanation, because every force they can feel directly involves touching something.
misconceptions.correction: Action at a distance is explained using the field. Each magnet sits in the field of the other, and the repulsion still happens with the air pumped away.

misconceptions.question: Does a magnet have a field when there is nothing nearby for it to attract?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The field is a property of the magnet and is there whether or not a second object is present.
misconceptions.misconception: A field only appears at the moment a second object is brought close enough to feel a force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fields are invisible, so students accept them only when there is an observable force to point at.
misconceptions.correction: The field tells you the force a second object would feel if it were placed there. It exists in advance; the second object only reveals it.

misconceptions.question: Which kinds of effect does physics analyse using fields?
misconceptions.misconception: Friction, air resistance and other contact forces are also analysed as field effects.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students group all forces together and do not separate contact forces from non-contact forces.
misconceptions.correction: Fields are used for the non-contact effects: electrical, magnetic and gravitational. Friction and air resistance act only where surfaces are in contact.

misconceptions.question: What has to be true for energy to be transferred by heating?
misconceptions.correct: There has to be a temperature difference between the two places.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is transferred by heating whenever an object is hot, whatever is around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat temperature as an absolute property of an object rather than something to compare with the surroundings.
misconceptions.correction: It is the difference that drives the transfer. Two objects at the same high temperature transfer no net energy to each other.

misconceptions.question: What drives charge to flow round a circuit?
misconceptions.correct: A potential difference across the component or the circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge flows because a large amount of charge is stored in the cell, so the amount of charge is what matters.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word charge appears in both ideas, and students picture a cell as a tank of charge that empties itself.
misconceptions.correction: The driver of change is the difference in potential, in the same way that a pressure difference drives gas flow and a temperature difference drives heating.

misconceptions.question: Is the extension of a spring proportional to the force for every force?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is directly proportional only up to the limit of proportionality.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the force always doubles the extension, however large the force becomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Class experiments usually stay within the proportional region, so students never see the graph bend.
misconceptions.correction: Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph curves and equal increases in force give larger increases in extension. The proportional model has a stated range of validity.

misconceptions.question: Are weight and mass the same quantity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Weight is directly proportional to mass, with gravitational field strength as the constant of proportionality.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are two names for the same quantity, just written in different units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech people give weight in kilograms, and on one planet the two numbers really are in a fixed ratio.
misconceptions.correction: Weight is a force measured in newtons and mass is measured in kilograms. Proportionality links them; it does not make them identical, as a change of planet shows.

misconceptions.question: Does any straight-line graph show a directly proportional relationship?
misconceptions.correct: No. The line must also pass through the origin.
misconceptions.misconception: Any straight line means that the two quantities are directly proportional.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'straight line' as the test for proportionality and drop the second half of the rule.
misconceptions.correction: A straight line with an intercept shows a constant rate of change, not proportionality. Doubling one quantity then does not double the other.

misconceptions.question: Are the key ideas assessed in the examinations?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They are embedded throughout the subject content and are assessed across all papers.
misconceptions.misconception: The key ideas are introductory reading for teachers and are never examined.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The key ideas are not set out as a teaching topic with their own content list, so students treat them as preamble.
misconceptions.correction: Because they are of universal application, questions on any topic and on any paper can require them.

misconceptions.question: Is a key idea the same thing as a detailed piece of subject content?
misconceptions.correct: No. A key idea is a way of thinking that recurs across many topics.
misconceptions.misconception: A key idea is just a single piece of subject content to be learned in one place — an especially big topic, a rule belonging to the topic that introduced it, a required practical, or a set of unit names — rather than a way of thinking that recurs across many topics.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate importance with the amount of detail they have to learn.
misconceptions.correction: A small number of key ideas describe a very wide range of phenomena. Their value lies in how widely they apply, not in how much detail they contain.

misconceptions.question: What is an equation in physics for?
misconceptions.correct: It expresses a physical law or model as a relationship between quantities.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation is only a recipe for getting a number out of a calculation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most classroom use of equations is substitution practice, so the relationship they express is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Writing weight = mass × gravitational field strength states that weight is proportional to mass. The equation carries the physics; the arithmetic is a consequence of it.

mcqs.stem: The specification says that diverse phenomena can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas. Which statement best describes a key idea in physics?

options.text: A way of thinking that recurs in many topics and describes a wide range of phenomena
options.rationale: A key idea is valuable because it applies across the whole subject, not because it is detailed.

options.text: An especially large and detailed topic that has to be revised in far more depth
options.rationale: Students equate importance with the amount of detail to be learned.

options.text: A rule that applies only inside the topic in which it was first taught
options.rationale: Revising topic by topic makes every idea look local to one topic.

options.text: A page of background reading that is never used in any examination paper
options.rationale: The key ideas are not a taught topic, so students dismiss them as preamble.

mcqs.stem: The key ideas are of universal application and are embedded throughout the subject content. What does this mean for the examinations?

options.text: They are printed for teachers and are never examined in any paper
options.rationale: m14: treats key ideas as teacher-only background reading that is never assessed.

options.text: They can be assessed in questions on any topic, on all papers
options.rationale: The specification states that the key ideas underpin the assessment and are assessed across all papers.

options.text: They are examined only in questions set for the higher tier
options.rationale: Students assume anything abstract must be higher tier only, but the key ideas apply at both tiers.

options.text: They are not examined, as they are not a taught topic
options.rationale: With no content list of its own, the section looks like guidance for teachers.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following does the specification list as a key idea in physics?

options.text: Learning the names of all the required practical activities
options.rationale: Practicals are prominent and separately listed, so students mistake them for key ideas.

options.text: Quoting every calculated answer to three significant figures
options.rationale: A working convention confused with a key idea; it is notation, not a way of explaining phenomena.

options.text: The use of models, such as the particle model of matter
options.rationale: The specification lists the use of models, as in the particle model of matter or the wave models of light and of sound.

options.text: Recalling the names of the SI base units in physics
options.rationale: Units are universal too, so students group them with the key ideas, but they are notation rather than explanation.

mcqs.stem: Why is the particle model of matter called a model?

options.text: Because it is a physical copy of matter built for classroom use
options.rationale: In everyday language a model is a scale object, so students look for a physical thing.

options.text: Because it is an idea that no evidence has yet been found for
options.rationale: Students hear 'model' as 'only a theory', meaning unsupported by evidence.

options.text: Because it applies to solids but not to liquids or gases
options.rationale: The particle model is usually met first with solids, so its range is underestimated.

options.text: Because it is a simplified way to explain and predict
options.rationale: A model is a simplified representation judged by how well it explains and predicts.

mcqs.stem: Light and sound are both described using a wave model. Which statement about these two models is correct?

options.text: Sound and light are both modelled as transverse waves through matter
options.rationale: m03: both waves drawn as wavy lines, so both wrongly labelled transverse.

options.text: Sound is modelled as a longitudinal wave and light as a transverse wave
options.rationale: The two wave models differ: sound oscillates along the direction of travel, light across it.

options.text: Sound and light are both modelled as transverse waves on a screen
options.rationale: The oscilloscope trace looks transverse, so students read it as a picture of the wave.

options.text: Each wave model is a real wavy object, like a small model plane
options.rationale: m01: a model is taken as a literal physical replica, like a toy plane.

mcqs.stem: A car on a straight road has a constant resultant force acting forwards. Using the idea of cause and effect, what is the effect of that force?

options.text: The car keeps moving at a steady speed while the force acts
options.rationale: Everyday pushing against friction gives a steady speed, so force is linked to speed.

options.text: The car gains mass steadily while the force is applied
options.rationale: Confuses which quantity changes; mass is a property, not an effect of a force.

options.text: The car accelerates for as long as the force acts on it
options.rationale: A resultant force is the cause and acceleration is the effect.

options.text: The car halts the instant the force is removed
options.rationale: Objects appear to stop when pushing stops, because friction is then unbalanced.

mcqs.stem: A sample of an unstable isotope emits alpha particles. Applying the idea of cause and effect, what is the cause of this emission?

options.text: A chemical reaction between the outer electrons
options.rationale: Most changes students meet are chemical, so decay is assumed to be chemical too.

options.text: The high temperature of the material around it
options.rationale: Heating speeds up most processes, so students expect it to speed up decay.

options.text: A collision with a nearby moving atom
options.rationale: Kinetic theory makes collisions the usual trigger, so students transfer that to decay.

options.text: A change inside the nucleus of the atom
options.rationale: The specification links changes in atomic nuclei to radioactive emissions.

mcqs.stem: Two magnets repel each other without touching. Which group of effects does physics analyse using the idea of a field?

options.text: Electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects
options.rationale: The specification names these three as the effects analysed using the field concept.

options.text: Gravitational, frictional and elastic contact effects
options.rationale: Students group all forces together and do not separate contact from non-contact.

options.text: Electrical, magnetic and thermal conduction effects
options.rationale: Conduction needs a material, which students confuse with a field acting through matter.

options.text: Magnetic, elastic push and near-contact effects
options.rationale: m07: field thought to exist only when a second object is brought near.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly applies the key idea that differences are the drivers of change?

options.text: Gas flows out of a cylinder when the gas inside has a large volume
options.rationale: Confuses the amount of gas with the pressure difference that actually drives the flow.

options.text: Energy is transferred by heating when an object is at a high temperature
options.rationale: Temperature is treated as absolute rather than compared with the surroundings.

options.text: Charge flows through a resistor when there is a potential difference across it
options.rationale: Potential difference is the electrical case of a difference driving a change.

options.text: Charge flows through a resistor when a large charge is stored in the cell
options.rationale: A cell is pictured as a tank of charge that empties itself round the circuit.

mcqs.stem: The weight of an object is directly proportional to its mass. What does this tell you?

options.text: A graph of weight against mass is a straight line with a positive intercept
options.rationale: Any straight line is taken as proportional, with the origin condition forgotten.

options.text: Weight and mass are the same quantity written in different units
options.rationale: Everyday speech gives weight in kilograms, which hides the distinction.

options.text: The graph is a straight line, which by itself proves the two are proportional
options.rationale: m13: any straight line is taken as sufficient proof of proportionality.

options.text: Doubling the mass doubles the weight in the same gravitational field
options.rationale: Proportionality means the two quantities change by the same factor, with g as the constant.

mcqs.stem: A student loads a spring with increasing weights and finds that extension is directly proportional to force. Which statement about this model is correct?

options.text: Doubling the force doubles the extension up to the limit of proportionality
options.rationale: The proportional model holds only within a stated range of validity.

options.text: Doubling the force doubles the extension for every force applied to the spring
options.rationale: Class experiments stay in the proportional region, so the limit is never seen.

options.text: Any straight-line graph shows extension is directly proportional to force
options.rationale: Proportionality is confused with a condition on the starting point of the graph.

options.text: Doubling the force still doubles the extension even past the elastic limit
options.rationale: m11: proportionality assumed to hold for any force, even beyond the limit.

mcqs.stem: The specification says that physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form. Which statement shows this key idea?

options.text: Rearranging an equation changes the physical law that it describes
options.rationale: Symbol manipulation is treated as altering the physics rather than the layout.

options.text: weight = mass × gravitational field strength is a relationship
options.rationale: The equation expresses the law that weight is proportional to mass, in the form the specification uses.

options.text: An equation is only a shortcut for doing the arithmetic quickly
options.rationale: Classroom use is mostly substitution, so the relationship expressed is easy to miss.

options.text: A description of a law in words is more precise than an equation
options.rationale: Students who find symbols hard assume that words carry the same information.
